# Pyelonephritis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Infectious kidney diseases > Pyelonephritis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Hi0KGf)

---

## Summary

Pyelonephritis is an infection of the <u>renal pelvis</u> and <u>parenchyma</u> that is usually associated with an ascending bacterial infection of the <u>bladder</u>. It occurs more commonly in women and <u>risk factors</u> include <u>pregnancy</u> and <u>urinary tract obstruction</u>. Patients typically present with flank <u>pain</u>, <u>costovertebral angle tenderness</u>, <u>fever</u>, and other features of <u>cystitis</u> (e.g., <u>dysuria</u>, frequency). <u>Urinalysis</u> shows <u>pyuria</u> and <u>bacteriuria</u>. <u>Urine cultures</u> should be taken in all patients before initiating treatment to identify the <u>pathogen</u> and possible <u>antibiotic</u> resistance. Early <u>empiric antibiotic treatment</u> is essential to avoid renal complications and <u>urosepsis</u>. Definitive treatment depends on the drug <u>sensitivities</u> of the causative <u>pathogen</u> and the patient's clinical profile (e.g., possible comorbidities).




See also “<u>Urinary tract infections</u>.”

---

## Etiology

* Usually caused by an ascending bacterial infection of the <u>bladder</u> (<u>cystitis</u>)

* Less commonly due to hematogenous spread of infection to the <u>kidney</u> (e.g., <u>infectious endocarditis</u>)

* Pathogens

* Gram-negative bacteria

* <u>Escherichia coli</u> (∼ 75–90% of cases; leading cause of pyelonephritis)

* <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u>

* <u>Klebsiella pneumoniae</u>

* <u>Proteus mirabilis</u>

* Gram-positive bacteria

* <u>Enterococcus faecalis</u>

* <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u>

* <u>Staphylococcus saprophyticus</u> [[2]](/library/uCYpFr)

* <u>Candida</u> infection (especially in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients) is possible

* Risk factors for pyelonephritis

* Most common in women because they have shorter urethras

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u> (potentially leading to pyonephrosis)

* Foreign bodies (e.g., indwelling urinary catheters or other urologic instrumentation)

* Anatomical abnormalities (e.g., <u>benign prostatic hyperplasia</u>, <u>vesicoureteral reflux</u>, <u>nephrolithiasis</u>, ureteral strictures)

* <u>Cystitis</u>

* Recent administration of <u>antibiotics</u> (possible <u>antibiotic</u> resistance)

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>;  (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)

* <u>Renal transplant</u>  [[3]](/library/dCcoIe0)[[4]](/library/VCcGIe0)

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Fever</u>, chills

* Flank <u>pain</u>

* Costovertebral angle tenderness: <u>pain</u> upon percussion of the flank (usually unilateral, may be bilateral)

* <u>Dysuria</u> as well as other <u>symptoms of cystitis</u> (e.g., frequency, urgency)

* <u>Weakness</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u> (<u>diarrhea</u> may also be present)

* Possible abdominal or <u>pelvic pain</u>





> [!TIP]
> Suspect pyelonephritis in any patient presenting with <u>fevers</u>, chills, and flank <u>pain</u>, irrespective of <u>lower urinary tract symptoms</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Pyelonephritis symptoms may overlap with those of other life-threatening causes of flank <u>pain</u> (see “<u>Differential diagnosis of pyelonephritis</u>”).




![Percussion of the Kidneys - Clinical Examination](media/small_60753b4cee68b.jpg)

Percussion of the Kidneys - Clinical Examination

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Pyelonephritis is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> that is supported by positive <u>urine culture</u>.

* Routine diagnostic workup should include <u>blood cultures</u> (2 sets), <u>urinalysis with microscopy</u>, and <u>urine culture</u> with susceptibilities.

* Check <u>CBC</u>, <u>BMP</u> for <u>signs of sepsis</u> and organ dysfunction.

* Consider imaging in patients with suspected <u>complicated pyelonephritis</u> or treatment failure.





### Laboratory tests




* <u>Urinalysis</u>  [[6]](/library/BRYz6K)

* Nonspecific findings of <u>UTI</u>

* <u>Pyuria</u> (positive esterase on <u>dipstick test</u>)

* <u>Leukocyturia</u> (<u>WBCs</u> > 5/hpf)

* <u>Bacteriuria</u>

* Positive nitrites on <u>dipstick test</u> indicate bacteria that convert <u>nitrates</u> to nitrites. [[9]](/library/xbbEDH)

* <u>Hematuria</u> (including <u>microhematuria</u>)

* Other findings

* <u>WBC casts</u>; : rare finding, but considered to be a strong indicator for pyelonephritis  [[6]](/library/BRYz6K)[[10]](/library/ysYdxq)

* Urine <u>pH</u> of ≥ 7.5–8.0: associated with <u>urease-producing organisms</u>  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)[[11]](/library/mbbV8H)[[12]](/library/5bbi8H)

* <u>Epithelial</u> cells > 5/hpf: suggests contamination.

* <u>Gram stain</u>: direct visualization of bacteria (seldom performed)

* <u>Urine culture</u> with susceptibilities

* Perform in all patients with suspected pyelonephritis to determine the <u>pathogen</u> and any associated drug resistance.

* ≥ 10<sup>5</sup> <u>colony-forming units</u>/mL suggests bacterial infection (See “<u>Urine culture</u>” for more details.) [[13]](/library/kIYm1q)[[14]](/library/bpbHLu)

* <u>Blood cultures</u> (2 sets): should be performed in all patients with suspected <u>complicated pyelonephritis</u>

* Urine <u>pregnancy test</u> in women of childbearing age

* Additional blood tests

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>leukocytosis</u>

* <u>Inflammatory markers</u>: ↑ <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: may be normal or show elevated <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u>





> [!TIP]
> Collect urine and <u>blood cultures</u> before administering <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u>.

### Imaging [[15]](/library/eCcxIe0)




#### Indications




* Imaging is not routinely indicated in patients with suspected acute <u>uncomplicated pyelonephritis</u>.

* Imaging serves to identify obstruction, <u>abscess</u>, or <u>emphysematous pyelonephritis</u>.

* Consider in the following situations: [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* <u>Complicated pyelonephritis</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u> or <u>septic shock</u>

* Known or suspected <u>nephrolithiasis</u>  [[16]](/library/eXbxCH)

* New decline in <u>eGFR</u> to < 40

* Recurrent pyelonephritis  [[5]](/library/9RYN6K)

* No response to therapy within 2 days





> [!TIP]
> CT is the imaging study of choice for assessing patients with suspected <u>complicated pyelonephritis</u> and ruling out differential diagnoses.




> [!WARNING]
> In the emergency department, <u>renal POCUS</u> may be helpful for quickly identifying <u>hydronephrosis</u>, but it does not preclude the need for CT in patients who require imaging. [[17]](/library/35YSPp)




#### CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with and without IV contrast  [[18]](/library/nbb78H)




Modality of choice in nonpregnant patients who need imaging




* CT findings in pyelonephritis 

* Renal <u>parenchyma</u> may appear normal (early) or <u>edematous</u> (<u>hypodense</u> areas)

* Infected <u>parenchyma</u> may be visible as;  wedge-shaped areas of streaky <u>contrast enhancement</u> (striated nephrogram).   [[18]](/library/nbb78H)

* CT findings in <u>urinary tract obstruction</u>

* <u>Hydroureter</u>, <u>hydronephrosis</u>

* <u>Nephrolithiasis</u>, <u>urolithiasis</u> (well-defined hyperintensities)

* Other findings that may be present

* Congenital abnormalities of the renal tract

* <u>Abscess</u>: intra-or extraparenchymal <u>hypodense</u> areas with peripheral <u>contrast enhancement</u>

* <u>Emphysematous pyelonephritis</u>: presence of gas within the renal <u>parenchyma</u>, collecting system or perinephric space [[19]](/library/g2bFSG)

* Hemorrhage in the <u>parenchyma</u> (<u>hyperdense</u> areas)





![Acute pyelonephritis and renal calculi](media/vx9g5r63sq44ecg0d5xa6d3a.jpg)

Acute pyelonephritis and renal calculi

![Chronic ureteral obstruction](media/kj60ba54ywxq8ymflvm5v6ei.jpg)

Chronic ureteral obstruction

![Ureter calculus with hydronephrosis](media/p5bcjk59ra8dkz51t5jip56f.jpg)

Ureter calculus with hydronephrosis




#### <u>Ultrasound of the kidneys</u> and <u>bladder</u> [[18]](/library/nbb78H)




* Indications: patients with <u>contraindications to CT</u> scan (e.g., <u>allergy</u> to contrast)

* Findings supportive of pyelonephritis 

* Renal enlargement

* Loss of corticomedullary differentiation

* <u>Edema</u> (<u>hypoechoic</u> regions)

* Hemorrhage (<u>hyperechoic</u> regions) in the <u>parenchyma</u>

* <u>Abscess</u>: thick-walled <u>hypoechoic</u> region

* Findings supportive of <u>urinary tract obstruction</u> 

* <u>Hydroureter</u>, <u>hydronephrosis</u>

* Thickened <u>bladder</u> wall

* High <u>bladder</u> <u>residual volume</u>

* <u>Prostate</u> enlargement

* Disadvantages: low <u>sensitivity</u> compared to CT, particularly in early acute infections [[18]](/library/nbb78H)





![Pyelonephritis](media/ehrd4titnjjofn6u31yhm2l3.jpg)

Pyelonephritis

![Hydronephrosis](media/fkyc2qx0ajxhg0ogerg06qmu.jpg)

Hydronephrosis




#### <u>MRI</u> abdomen and <u>pelvis</u>




* Indications

* Patients with <u>contraindications to CT</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u> [[18]](/library/nbb78H)

* Findings: similar to <u>CT scan</u> (See “CT abdomen and <u>pelvis</u> with and without IV contrast.”) [[18]](/library/nbb78H)





![Striated nephrogram](media/tnqt0gvjyeuls2a5h3s0mb6y.jpg)

Striated nephrogram




#### Additional imaging modalities




The following are rarely used, as CT, <u>MRI</u>, and <u>ultrasound</u> are more widely available.




* <u>Intravenous pyelogram</u> (IVP)

* Indications: suspected obstruction or congenital abnormality [[20]](/library/ZXbZ9H)

* Characteristic findings  [[18]](/library/nbb78H)

* Enlarged <u>kidney</u>

* Striated nephrogram

* Delayed nephrogram and delayed calyceal opacification time  [[21]](/library/obb0uH)

* Dilation or effacement of the <u>collecting duct</u>

* <u>DMSA scan</u> [[18]](/library/nbb78H)

* Indications: children with suspected pyelonephritis  [[22]](/library/dXboCH)

* Characteristic findings: Acute pyelonephritis is visible as focal or <u>global</u> areas of decreased uptake.

* Additional imaging to consider

* <u>Voiding cystourethrogram</u>: used to diagnose <u>vesicoureteral reflux</u> [[23]](/library/KbbUuH)

* <u>Urodynamic testing</u>: to exclude <u>neurogenic bladder</u> or <u>subvesical obstruction</u>





![Obstructing ureteral calculus](media/kykliektgusg5jshq0ev2v0a.jpg)

Obstructing ureteral calculus

## Pathology

* Acute pyelonephritis

* Most commonly affects the cortex (spares <u>glomeruli</u> and vessels)

* <u>Purulent inflammation</u> of the <u>interstitium</u> with destruction of the <u>parenchyma</u>, the renal tubules, and, in some cases, the <u>renal pelvis</u>

* <u>Histology</u>

* Neutrophilic infiltration of the renal tubules and the <u>interstitium</u>

* Sparing of the <u>glomeruli</u> and intrarenal vessels

* <u>Chronic pyelonephritis</u>

* Chronic inflammatory changes with rough, asymmetric scarring and <u>fibrosis</u> of the corticomedullary junction

* Blunted calyces from recurrent urinary reflux

* <u>Histology</u>: <u>eosinophilic casts</u> in the tubules that resemble <u>thyroid</u> tissue with coloid (<u>thyroidization</u> of the <u>kidney</u>)

* Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis

* A rare form of <u>chronic pyelonephritis</u> characterized by chronic destructive <u>granuloma</u> formation

* Associated with <u>Proteus mirabilis</u> and <u>Escherichia coli</u> infections

* Large, irregular, yellow-orange masses on gross examination of the <u>kidney</u> (may be mistaken for a true renal <u>neoplasm</u>)

* <u>Histology</u>: granulomatous tissue with lipid-laden foamy <u>macrophages</u> and <u>multinucleated giant cells</u>

## Differential diagnoses

See also “<u>Differential diagnoses of acute abdomen</u>” and “<u>Differential diagnoses of acute back pain</u>.”




* Other <u>kidney</u> and <u>urinary tract</u> disorders

* <u>Lower UTIs</u>

* <u>Renal colic</u>

* <u>Renal vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Renal infarct</u>

* Other intraabdominal, <u>retroperitoneal</u>, and <u>pelvic</u> disorders

* <u>Psoas abscess</u>

* <u>Splenic infarct</u> or <u>abscess</u>

* <u>Retroperitoneal hematoma</u> or infection

* <u>Acute cholecystitis</u>

* <u>Appendicitis</u>

* <u>Diverticulitis</u>

* <u>Pelvic inflammatory disease</u>

* <u>Endometriosis</u>

* Disorders outside the abdomen, <u>pelvis</u>, and <u>retroperitoneum</u>

* Musculoskeletal disorders (e.g., spinal, paraspinal)

* <u>Pleural empyema</u>

* <u>Pulmonary infarct</u>

* <u>Shingles</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

<u>Antibiotic therapy</u>, source control, and <u>supportive care</u> are the mainstays of <u>treatment of pyelonephritis</u>. The choice of <u>empiric antibiotic</u> regimen should be guided by the risk of infection with resistant organisms (i.e., complicated vs. <u>uncomplicated pyelonephritis</u>) and <u>antibiotics</u> should be tailored as soon as culture results become available. Consider specialist consultation in cases of <u>complicated pyelonephritis</u>, especially if <u>urinary tract obstruction</u> is suspected.




![Management of acute pyelonephritis](media/kfhf7cm7pxiudmjgxnhkrpif.jpg)

Management of acute pyelonephritis




### <u>Uncomplicated pyelonephritis</u> [[5]](/library/9RYN6K)[[7]](/library/u9Yp6r)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)




* Empiric antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated pyelonephritis [[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* Most patients can be treated with an oral <u>fluoroquinolone</u> (e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u>;  DOSAGE, <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE) for 5–7 days  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)[[25]](/library/wRYh6K)

* Alternatives

* <u>Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole</u> DOSAGE, for 10–14 days (only recommended if susceptibility is known)  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* <u>Amoxicillin/clavulanate</u> DOSAGE for 10–14 days [[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* <u>Cefpodoxime</u> DOSAGE for 10–14 days [[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* Consider a single dose of a broad-spectrum parenteral <u>antibiotic</u> prior to the administration of oral <u>antibiotics</u>, especially when the local rates of drug-resistant <u>E. coli</u> are unknown or known to be > 10%. [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE

* OR <u>gentamicin</u> DOSAGE [[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)[[25]](/library/wRYh6K)

* <u>Supportive care</u>

* Encourage the patient to drink adequate amounts of fluids.

* Consider an IV fluid bolus in patients with <u>dehydration</u>. [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* <u>Analgesia</u> for <u>pain</u> (see “<u>Pain management</u>”)  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* <u>Antiemetics</u> in patients with <u>nausea and vomiting</u> (e.g., <u>ondansetron</u> DOSAGE) [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* Additional considerations

* Outpatient treatment is generally appropriate.

* If there is no response within 48 hours of starting <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u>:

* Consider imaging to evaluate for <u>urinary tract obstruction</u> or formation of <u>renal abscess</u> (see “Diagnostics”).

* Check <u>urine culture</u> results and adjust treatment accordingly.  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* Repeat <u>urine culture</u> (i.e., “test for cure”) is not routinely indicated. [[5]](/library/9RYN6K)





> [!TIP]
> A single dose of a broad-spectrum parenteral <u>antibiotic</u> prior to the administration of oral <u>antibiotics</u> is recommended when local rates of <u>E. coli</u> resistance are > 10% (or unknown) or if <u>trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole</u> is used empirically.




### <u>Complicated pyelonephritis</u> [[5]](/library/9RYN6K)[[7]](/library/u9Yp6r)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)




Patients with complicated acute pyelonephritis should be admitted to the hospital and started on parenteral <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u> as soon as possible. [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)



* The choice of <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u> should be decided based on:

* Clinical severity (i.e., presence of <u>sepsis</u>)

* The presence of <u>risk factors</u> for infection with multidrug-resistant bacteria  [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* Age ≥ 65 years

* Recent stay in hospital or long-term care facility

* Recent <u>antibiotic</u> use

* Indwelling <u>urinary tract</u> devices

* Known abnormalities of the urological tract or <u>urinary tract obstruction</u>

* Previous resistant infection

* Recent travel to an area with high <u>antibiotic</u> resistance (e.g., Asia, Mexico)

| Patient characteristics | <u>Antibiotic</u> regimens to consider |  |

| <u>Enterococcus</u> or <u>MRSA</u> suspected | <br><br>* Consider adding <u>vancomycin</u>. DOSAGE<br><br>* OR if there is concern for <u>VRE</u>, add one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Daptomycin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* <u>Linezolid</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> |  |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Fluoroquinolone</u> monotherapy should be avoided in severely ill patients with <u>complicated pyelonephritis</u> due to the high <u>prevalence</u> of <u>fluoroquinolone</u>-resistant pathogens!




* <u>Supportive care</u>

* <u>Analgesics</u> as needed (see “<u>Pain management</u>”)

* <u>Antiemetics</u> as needed

* Additional considerations

* Aggressive IV resuscitation for patients with <u>sepsis</u> (see “<u>IV fluid therapy</u>”)

* Source control: Consider imaging to identify <u>urinary obstruction</u> (see “Diagnostics” above).

* Specialist consultations

* Urology consultation if <u>renal abscess</u> or obstruction is present/suspected

* Nephrology consultation in patients with <u>AKI</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> derangements, need for <u>hemodialysis</u>

* Critical care consultation if <u>septic shock</u> is present

* Management of complications

* <u>Abscess</u>

* <u>Abscess</u> < 3 cm and no <u>signs of sepsis</u>: no drainage necessary

* <u>Abscess</u> ≥ 3 cm and/or <u>signs of sepsis</u> present: percutaneous drainage of <u>abscess</u>

* Life-threatening <u>urosepsis</u>: urology/<u>surgery</u> consultation for possible <u>nephrectomy</u> [[27]](/library/WM0Png)[[28]](/library/-RYDpK)

* <u>Shock</u>: aggressive <u>fluid resuscitation</u>, <u>vasopressors</u> (see “<u>Shock</u>”)

* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u>: emergent urology and IR consultation for <u>ureteral stenting</u> or <u>percutaneous nephrostomy</u>

* Subsequent management

* Duration of <u>antibiotic therapy</u>: 10–14 days [[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> should be adjusted once blood and <u>urine culture</u> <u>sensitivity</u> reports are available.

* Consider repeat <u>urine culture</u> in pregnant women and those with recurrent pyelonephritis 2–4 days after completion of the <u>antibiotic</u> course. [[5]](/library/9RYN6K)[[29]](/library/pbbLuH)

* Identify and treat the underlying cause.





> [!TIP]
> Patients with concurrent <u>urinary tract obstruction</u> are at very high risk of clinical deterioration and require immediate intervention to remove the obstruction.




### Admission criteria [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)




Consider inpatient management if any of the following are present:




* <u>Complicated pyelonephritis</u>

* Potential difficulties in following outpatient care and follow-up instructions

* No suitable oral <u>antibiotic</u>

* Ongoing <u>hypovolemia</u>

* Persistent <u>nausea and vomiting</u>

---

## Complications

* <u>Urosepsis</u>, <u>septic shock</u>

* <u>Perinephric abscess</u>; , <u>renal abscess</u>

* <u>Renal papillary necrosis</u>

* Emphysematous pyelonephritis [[18]](/library/nbb78H)

* Rare form of pyelonephritis characterized by gas formation within and around the <u>kidney</u>

* Most common in patients with poorly controlled <u>diabetes</u> or <u>immunodeficiency</u>

* Typically caused by <u>E. coli</u> or <u>K. pneumoniae</u>

* Treatment includes IV <u>antibiotics</u>, percutaneous drainage, and, in some cases, <u>nephrectomy</u>.

* Recurrent bacterial pyelonephritis 

* If recurrence is caused by the same organism despite adequate treatment, then prolong the course of <u>antibiotics</u> for 6 weeks.

* If a new <u>pathogen</u> is identified, change <u>antibiotics</u> accordingly and treat for 2 weeks.

* <u>Atrophic</u> <u>kidneys</u>

* End-stage renal disease (<u>ESRD</u>): if both <u>kidneys</u> are affected, the patient has a <u>single kidney</u>, or the other <u>kidney</u> has been damaged by a different pathology





> [!TIP]
> Rule out <u>urosepsis</u> in elderly patients with <u>altered mental status</u>!




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Special patient groups

### Pyelonephritis in pregnancy [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)




* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* The risk of pyelonephritis is increased during <u>pregnancy</u>.

* As many as one-third of pregnant women with <u>asymptomatic bacteriuria</u> will progress to develop pyelonephritis (if left untreated).

* One of the most common <u>complications of pregnancy</u>, with potentially severe consequences for both mother and fetus   [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)

* Diagnosis: See “Diagnostics” above; use <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> for imaging. [[30]](/library/-gVDBF0)

* Treatment [[1]](/library/jbb_tH)[[24]](/library/C9Yqpr)

* Hospitalization is recommended; definitive indications for hospitalization are: [[31]](/library/Yo1n030)

* <u>Signs of sepsis</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u> (e.g., due to <u>vomiting</u>)

* Contractions

* A third- or fourth-generation <u>cephalosporin</u> for 7–10 days, such as:

* <u>Cefotaxime</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE

* In severe pyelonephritis (<u>immunocompromised</u> patients or poor urine output), consider one of the following for 10–14 days:

* <u>Piperacillin/tazobactam</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ticarcillin</u>

* Parenteral <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u> are recommended at least until the patient is afebrile, after which transition to oral <u>antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporins</u>) is possible. [[31]](/library/Yo1n030)

* See “<u>Antibiotics during pregnancy</u>” for additional drugs and dosages.

* <u>Secondary prevention</u>: Monthly <u>urine culture</u> or prophylactic <u>nitrofurantoin</u> DOSAGE until 4–6 weeks postpartum is recommended, as the recurrence rate of <u>pyelonephritis in pregnancy</u> is 25%. [[32]](/library/ibbJtH)





> [!TIP]
> All asymptomatic cases of <u>bacteriuria</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> must be treated to prevent the development of pyelonephritis.




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>fluoroquinolones</u>, <u>trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole</u>, and <u>aminoglycosides</u> in pregnant women!




### <u>Acute pyelonephritis in children</u>




See "<u>Urinary tract infection in children and adolescents</u>."

## Chronic pyelonephritis

* Description: a consequence of recurrent or persistent acute pyelonephritis

* Predisposing factors

* <u>Vesicoureteric reflux</u>

* <u>Urinary tract obstruction</u> (e.g., <u>nephrolithiasis</u>, <u>neurogenic bladder</u>)

* Clinical features

* Nonspecific (mild <u>fever</u>, <u>anorexia</u>, <u>malaise</u>)

* Abdominal or flank <u>pain</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Urinalysis</u>: <u>pyuria</u>, <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>WBC casts</u>

* Imaging (<u>ultrasound</u>, <u>intravenous urogram</u>): corticomedullary scarring (mainly upper pole), blunt/clubbed renal calyces

* <u>Biopsy</u>: thyroidization of the <u>kidney</u> (see ''Pathology'')

* Treatment

* Treat the underlying cause.

* <u>Antibiotics</u>
